coverage.method: Complete page text extracted from approved chunk PDFs in source order; PDF rendering separately recorded where layout or source uncertainty requires it.

findings.analytical_note: New deputies were chiefly propertied lawyers with substantial practical local revolutionary experience, despite predecessors’ dismissive descriptions. Local conflict over nonjurors helped determine their priorities.

The contrast between closed Feuillant meetings and public Jacobin debate explains movement of ambitious deputies and the destruction of Feuillant influence; royal reconciliation initially appeared plausible.

Brissot’s attack on émigrés escalated toward threats against their protectors. The royal veto was constitutional and had defensible stated grounds, yet fed conspiracy suspicions; actual queenly correspondence had different objectives from the supposed committee’s protection of émigrés.
Avignon violence and provincial religious conflict framed renewed oath, surveillance, pension-loss and expulsion measures; Louis vetoed the decree despite deputies’ fears.

reader_access_routes: Lafayette and Narbonne: army and domestic order
findings.analytical_note: Distinct incompatible groups supported war: court hopes of rescue, generals’ domestic authority, and Brissotin national regeneration and exposure of traitors. Compliance by Rhenish electors removed the original grievance but did not halt momentum.

Robespierre foresaw either military dictatorship after victory or counter-revolution after defeat and located danger at home. His isolation matters alongside the otherwise differently placed Feuillant opposition.

Vienna mistook French restraint for successful intimidation, while French deputies read threats as proof of conspiracy. Ministerial crisis, Leopold’s death and a warmongering ministry culminated in war with Francis as king of Hungary and Bohemia, before imperial election.

reader_access_routes: Defensive war: promises and later breach
findings.analytical_note: The declaration promised no conquest and respect for other peoples’ liberty and property; the author explicitly anticipates broken pledges. War also diverted attention while domestic crises multiplied.

Civil conflict and inconsistent metropolitan policies helped form the context for the slave uprising. Communication delays made responses obsolete; antislavery commitments and port dependence on slavery created distinct political embarrassments.

Colonial upheaval produced a sugar shock and female-led forced sales. Paris’s grain provisioning reduced surrounding reserves, while currency and exchange depreciation raised prices; these are different mechanisms, not a single food-shortage cause.

Regional political rivalries and attacks on counter-revolutionary centers preceded drowning rumors that triggered rural attacks. Doyle cautiously infers from targets that peasants feared reversal of 1789; retain that uncertainty.

The battle hymn first accompanied war enthusiasm. The guillotine was introduced as efficient, egalitarian and humane punishment after retention of capital punishment, initially for an ordinary criminal; Guillotin proposed but did not invent the machine.
Initial invasion failed through panic and indiscipline; reverses unleashed scapegoating and emergency measures. Preserve military and domestic consequences as separately retrievable treatments.

Vetoes and dismissal of ministers precipitated planned popular intimidation. Louis’s refusal, initial sympathy for him and Lafayette’s abortive intervention distinguish the failed June journée from August’s overthrow.

Popular societies widened participation beyond active citizens; shortages, price-control agitation and war anxiety revived organization. Continued sectional sessions and later suspension of citizen distinctions made effective insurrection possible.

Volunteer mobilization and provincial contingents sustained radical Parisian politics despite veto of the camp. Brunswick’s threats accelerated arming and political inclusion of formerly passive citizens.

Brissotins wanted ministers restored and recoiled from overthrow, alienating insurgents. The new Commune directed assault; royal flight, Swiss resistance, National Guard defection and ensuing killings ended effective monarchy and subordinated the legislature.

The legislature formally appointed ministers but the Commune held power. New tribunal and political executions, Lafayette’s escape, and detention of the royal family were separate consequences of August.

Surveillance, exit restrictions, priest arrests and house searches filled prisons amid military emergency. Fear that departing volunteers’ families would face conspirators linked mobilization to demands for preventive violence.

Military panic triggered prison killings aided and paid for by the Commune; improvised trials also acquitted prisoners. Most dead were common criminals, alongside priests and political prisoners; factional blame and fear of repetition outlived the event.
Valmy combined national enthusiasm, superior gun quality and pre-revolutionary technical training. Prussian negotiations and withdrawal show the military opening’s diplomatic significance.

reader_access_routes: Manhood suffrage: exclusions and indirect voting
findings.analytical_note: Convention elections broadened suffrage while excluding servants and unemployed and retaining two stages; low participation and experienced deputies qualify claims of democratic renewal. Legal and propertied dominance continued with a small artisan presence.

Evidence discoveries and competing constitutional arguments framed disposition of the king. Saint-Just and Robespierre treated popular judgment as already complete; deputies’ legal training favored a hearing, and the king’s demeanor affected opinion without determining innocence.

The appeal dispute concerned provincial review and fears of civil war. Separate votes addressed guilt, referendum, penalty and reprieve; immediate death was the largest penalty group, while other deputies favored conditional death or imprisonment.
Execution closed off compromise but was a challenge rather than uncomplicated victory, creating more enemies and strengthening existing ones both internationally and probably within France.

qualifications: Source chronology requires preservation: p. 193 links the Convention meeting and first republican act to the day of Valmy (20 September), while p. 194 explicitly dates abolition of monarchy to 21 September and the republican era to 22 September. Do not silently reconcile with outside history.
Peasant motives on p. 183 and influence of intimidation on execution votes on p. 196 are qualified inferences.
